newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: League table of world polluters.
newsitem.headline: League table of world polluters.

text.p: Major industrial nations, especially the United States, face attack at a U.N. Earth Summit this week for polluting the planet with greenhouse gases that cause global warming.

The United States, China, Russia, Japan and Germany are the world's biggest polluters, spewing out about 3.2 billion tons a year or half of the planet's carbon emissions from fuels like oil and coal, says the Washington-based Worldwatch Institute.

Share of world's emissions by percentage in 1995 are: United States, 23 percent or 1.39 billion tons; China 13.9 percent or 807 million tons; Russia 7.2 percent or 437 million tons; Japan 5 percent or 302 million tons; and Germany 3.8 percent or 234 million tons.

Share of world's emissions calculated on a per capita basis in 1995 are: United States 5.3 tons; Russia 2.9 tons; Japan 2.4 tons; Germany 2.9 tons. The figures for key developing countries are : China 0.7; Brazil 0.4 tons; and both India and Indonesia at 0.3 tons.

Emissions growth in percentage between 1990 and 1995: United States 6.2 percent; Russia minus 27.7 percent; Japan 8.7 percent; Germany minus 10.2 percent; China 27.5 percent; India 27.7 percent; Indonesia 38.8 percent and Brazil 19.8 percent.

The fall in emissions in Russia is attributed to a collapse in its industries, particularly the energy-intensive ones, since the fall of the Soviet Union. In Germany, the absorption of the former communist east into a united country allowed Bonn to close down numerous industries, especially coal plants.
